maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I wish to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. In the light of the public debate now taking place in Canada and in the United States concerning the proposal to construct an oil supply line via pipeline in Alaska and by ocean tanker to United States west coast markets, and arising out of the statement in Washington yesterday attributed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources offering the Mackenzie Valley route as a possible alternative to the Alaska TAPS pipeline route, such statement implying the feasibility of the Mackenzie Valley route and the offer as expressing government policy without public examination of the consequences and ramifications of such a plan, I move, seconded by the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau):
That this House is of the opinion that the government should make the necessary arrangements for a full debate in government time to discuss the whole question of the desirability of constructing oil and/or gas pipelines along the Mackenzie River valley from the Arctic coast to southern Canada and the effect of such an undertaking on, among other things, the ecology of the region, the rights of native peoples, the Canadian economy, the type of ownership thereof and by whom, international trade and Canada's foreign relations.

BROADCASTING-RESULTS OF EFFORTS TO PROVIDE MORE POSSIBILITIES OF COLLABORATION AND EXCHANGE
speechtext: What are the concrete results, to date, of the intensified efforts to provide more possibilities of joint collaboration and exchange, either on a dubbing basis or on a joint production basis with separate sound tracks referred to by Dr. Davidson on June 4, 1970 before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts?

subtopic: BROADCASTING-RESULTS OF EFFORTS TO PROVIDE MORE POSSIBILITIES OF COLLABORATION AND EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows:
The CBC's Program Council, under the chairmanship of the Vice-President, Programming, has the responsibility of promoting the exchange of program material and joint collaboration in production of programs and coverage of events wherever and whenever this is considered desirable. The Program Council includes among its members the Vice-Presidents and General Managers of the French and English language divisions.
A joint program planning group, consisting of senior officers from both French and English services and working under the aegis of the Program Council meets regularly to further inter-service collaboration and to examine specific program ideas and projects which lend themselves to joint production arrangements. Film properties are reviewed with a view to the possibility of use by both language services (including the requirement of dubbing). News, sports, music, special events and documentary programs generally afford the best opportunities for effective use of the same CBC program material by the two language services.
Examples of collaboration between the two language services in the coverage of events include Expo 67 (Montreal): Canada Games (Halifax) 1969; Commonwealth Games (Edinburgh) 1970; Expo 70 (Tokyo); Saskatoon Winter Games (1971); and many others. Joint productions, or dual use by the two networks of the same program material (with adaptations) include the d'Iberville series and the ballet Carmina Burana. Imported programs such as "The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau" and "The Forsyte Saga" have been scheduled on both CBC English and French TV networks.
Material used on the French network public affairs program "Format 60" has also been used on the English network's "Weekend". The well-known French network commentator Pierre Nadeau has been engaged to do special reporting for "Weekend". The current Canadian TV serial, "Adventures in Rainbow Country" has been converted for broadcast on the French network under the title "Au pays de l'arc-en-ciel".
Programs in the music field include a concert devoted to the music of Manuel de Falla; a concert of Canadian music; the opera "Hansel and Gretel"; a Glenn Gould program; the Canada Day program broadcast from the National Arts Centre July 1st; between 40 and 50 programs included under the series title "Son et Images" in French and "Music to See" in English.
Consideration is currently being given to the conversion of the twice repeated English play "Charbonneau and the Chef" for use on the French radio network, and plans are also being developed for future public affairs series to be scheduled by both French and English services, covering such subjects as pollution, the Arctic, science and technology. Looking further ahead plans are being developed jointly by the two networks for joint coverage of such future events as the Summer Olympics (Munich) 1972: the Winter Olympics (Sapporo, Japan) 1972 and the 1976 Summer Olympics (Montreal).

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 MANPOWER PROVISION OF EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 MANPOWER PROVISION OF EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
Subject to your decision, Mr. Speaker, I propose to ask leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, that during the latter part of this month and during the months of April, May and June at least 1,300,000 students will leave their high schools and colleges and will be seeking either temporary or permanent employment. This massive influx on the labour market will greatly aggravate the existing problem of unemployment in the immediate future.
It is for this reason that an immediate discussion of this matter is urgently required in order to assist the government in providing appropriate plans at the earliest possible moment to meet this emergency. If you agree that this matter is proper to be discussed, Mr. Speaker, I shall ask leave of the House to move that this House adjourn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 MANPOWER PROVISION OF EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Oxford has filed the notice required under Standing Order 26. His statement proposes a debate on the subject of unemployment, with particular reference to the fact that a considerable number of students and young people will be leaving schools or universities in the months of April, May and June of this year. While the matter is one of concern to the House and of national interest, and while the situation is urgent, I would hesitate very much before suggesting an emergency debate under Standing Order 26.
Hon. members are aware that during the past few weeks we have had a number of debates on the general subject of unemployment. There were two days of budget debate on February 10 and 11. Still more recently, on February 25 the House considered a supply motion and the debate which ensued on that motion was related primarily to the problem of unemployment.
I think it is relevant also to the decision which must be made by the Chair that the House on December 15 last considered a motion proposed by the hon. member for Lotbiniere. That motion, as well as an amendment moved by the hon. member for Vegreville dealt precisely with the problem raised in the motion which would be proposed by the hon. member for Oxford. I might indicate to hon. members that the situation might be different if the motion dealt more precisely with the situation to be faced by students who are looking for summer employment. It may well be that a time will arrive when such a debate should take place within the terms of a supply motion, in connection with a statement on motions, or by way of an emergency debate.
After considering the matter very seriously and with every sympathy possible, it seems to me that the terms of the statement put forward by the hon. member are per-

March 3, 1971
Motions for Papers
haps a bit too wide, and that the debate which would result under the terms of the motion as presented to the House would be very much the same as the debates we have had during the past few weeks. Although I have given the matter serious thought and have considered it with every possible sympathy, for these reasons I do not think that at this time at least, there should be a debate on the motion in the terms proposed by the hon. member for Oxford under Standing Order 26.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 MANPOWER PROVISION OF EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Prime Minister in reply to a number of questions I have asked in the last two weeks has indicated that the government is presently considering plans to deal with this matter. The fact that these plans have not been forthcoming and that time is running very short may perhaps distinguish my request for a special debate from the other debates which have taken place in respect of student unemployment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 MANPOWER PROVISION OF EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext: Of course the hon. member is not raising a point of order but rather he is debating the decision of the Chair. The Standing Order says precisely that there should not be a debate on the decision of the Chair. I can assure the hon. member that I have taken that point under serious consideration. I have suggested to him that had the motion dealt precisely with the question of summer employment for students, rather than the fact that 1,300,000 young people will come onto the labour market in a month or so, there might have been more justification for a debate at this time. At the same time, I could add that I might have thought it was a bit premature. As I have said, I have considered all aspects of the matter as sympathetically as possible and, in view of all the circumstances I did not think that an emergency debate should be held under the terms of Standing Order 26.

speechtext: I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister. Since over the past few years we have been faced every spring with more young people coming on the job market in an atmosphere of uncertainty and apprehension, and as the time has now come to have an intelligent, integrated and permanent solution to the problem of student employment, would the Acting Prime Minister and his colleagues consider the constitution of a federal-provincial task force to study both long and short-range solutions to this problem so that governments may begin to meet their responsibilities to the young people of this country?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TASK FORCE TO STUDY STUDENT EMPLOYMENT PROBLEM
speechtext: I will at least agree with my hon. friend that I do not think we can look upon this problem as one that will come on us without notice from year to year. I am satisfied, and I think members of this government are, that there will have to be a program from year to year in the future unless, of course-and this is one of the problems that is raised-we change our university year and provide for the education of students throughout the year rather than leaving a big gap in the summer time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TASK FORCE TO STUDY STUDENT EMPLOYMENT PROBLEM
speechtext: Order, please. I will recognize the hon. member for Egmont on a supplementary question. I take the liberty of mentioning to hon. members that a number of members would like to ask supplementary questions on this subject, but we should not have an excessive number of supplementary questions on the first subject raised because then we will run short of time. For the moment the Chair will recognize the hon. member for Egmont.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TASK FORCE TO STUDY STUDENT EMPLOYMENT PROBLEM

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT
speechtext: I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. In view of the fact that the student employment situation this summer will more than likely aggravate the intolerable unemployment problem at this time and for the future, can the minister now state whether he is prepared to give the House a definite indication of when he will be bringing in his legislation dealing with unemployment insurance?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT
speechtext: Being as definite as I can, I would anticipate that the legislation will be tabled very shortly.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT
speechtext: Since the minister and his colleagues have continually stated in the past month that this legislation would be brought in very shortly, which to me means very little, would the minister advise whether he indicated to the Canadian Labour Congress any reasons for not bringing in immediate relief by way of widening accessibility to unemployment insurance benefits and increasing the amounts in order to help alleviate this very serious situation-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT
speechtext: Created by the government.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT
speechtext: -created by the government?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can just say very shortly that I think the hon. member, as a member of the standing committee, knows that it is the intention of the government and of the proposed legislation to begin phasing in the new plan as of July 1, and I have no reason to believe the bill will not be tabled in sufficient time to make this possible. In so far as extending the benefit period and raising the benefits is concerned, this is another matter. It is a question of whether people who are unemployed for a long period of time should be helped through unemployment insurance or through other social policies.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT

maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-APPLICATION BY INDUSTRY TO ENERGY BOARD-ECOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-APPLICATION BY INDUSTRY TO ENERGY BOARD-ECOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources arising out of reports of his

March 3, 1971
Inquiries of the Ministry
visit to Washington yesterday. Has he publicly invited the oil industry to make an application to the National Energy Board to construct a pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley to the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-APPLICATION BY INDUSTRY TO ENERGY BOARD-ECOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not issued an invitation in those terms, but I have pointed out to my American counterparts the fact that the line to Valdez, which would mean tanker carriage of oil down the Pacific coast, would be ecologically very dangerous, and that it might be preferable to consider the Mackenzie Valley line and make an application to the National Energy Board in the normal course, at which time the economic and ecological considerations would be carefully considered during the determination of such application.

maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-APPLICATION BY INDUSTRY TO ENERGY BOARD-ECOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
speechtext: In view of the minister's reported statement in Washington that the Mackenzie route would be advisable from the standpoint of ecology, may I ask the minister the basis for this statement in view of the fact that on February 23 the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development stated that the ecological studies regarding this route had not yet been completed? I am therefore asking the minister on what basis has he decided that this would be a safer route in view of the fact that the studies have not been completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-APPLICATION BY INDUSTRY TO ENERGY BOARD-ECOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
speechtext: I am, of course, not responsible for press reports even though I am responsible for many other things. My statement was to the effect that there was very great concern about the possibility of marine disaster, that there has been a three-year study by the Mackenzie Valley pipeline group in regard to pipeline safety at Inuvik, and that the question of the safety of such a pipeline would be considered at any National Energy Board hearing. Certainly I think that in that regard I am on all fours with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-APPLICATION BY INDUSTRY TO ENERGY BOARD-ECOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
speechtext: In view of the statement the minister has just made that he has advised the oil industry to apply to the National Energy Board to construct such a pipeline, and in view of the fact that the National Energy Board is competent to deal with energy matters, who will make the decision with respect to the ecological matters? Is this a government decision, or is the minister now going to delegate to the National Energy Board the power to make decisions with regard to the ecology of the northern region?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-APPLICATION BY INDUSTRY TO ENERGY BOARD-ECOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
speechtext: I believe if my hon. friend will read the National Energy Board Act he will find that the question of the safety of the pipeline, in other words, the protection of the ecology, is very much one of the relevant issues in any application to the National Energy Board for the construction of a pipeline. Therefore in the first instance the Board does make that decision, along with other questions relevant to the application, and thereafter it must be ratified or denied by the government.

maintopic: CONTROL OF POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CONTROL OF POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was going to say we did not believe there was more than one of the minister, but when he talked to his counterparts in the United States and extended his invitation to the oil industry did he give any indication as to who would have control of this pipeline going through Canada? Has the minister given any indication to the oil industry that this pipeline would have to be controlled by Canadian interests, and if he has not given such indication what is the position of the government on this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: CONTROL OF POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I affirmed the announcement made by myself and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in August of last year, in which the conditions for the construction of such a pipeline were very clearly outlined both with respect to control by regulatory authorities on the Canadian side and with respect to ecological control, and in particular with respect to the fact that Canadian resources would have to have access to such a pipeline if it were built. That is still the government's position which was affirmed by me at my meeting in Washington yesterday.

maintopic: CONTROL OF POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE
speechtext: Am I to assume from the minister's reply that he said nothing about ownership?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, to judge from what has happened in the Soviet Union, and I would not want to take full credit for what has happened-

subtopic: CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, March 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benson that Bill C-219, to establish the Canada Development Corporation, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs and the amendment thereto of Mr. Baldwin (P. 3894).

subtopic: CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I called it ten o'clock last night, I indicated that I approved the major objectives set out for the Canada Development Corporation which are to develop strong Canadian controlled and managed corporations in the private sector of the economy and to provide broader opportunities for Canadians to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada.

March 3, 1971

I also said I was confident that the CDC would play an important role in future Canadian development and that it could contribute to improving Canadian competitiveness in world markets and in the arrangements for corporation rationalization and amalgamations in which we expect it to take part. By stimulating and encouraging such changes in Canadian industry, the Canada Development Corporation will strengthen our industrial structure and consequently render it less vulnerable to foreign take-overs.
Having said that, I wish to express reservations about the lack of specifics in this bill with regard to natural resource development. I realize that northern development and resource development are part of the bill's objects, but several features of the bill convince me that it was drafted by people who were manufacturing industry-oriented rather than resource-oriented. Certainly, mineral and hydrocarbon resource development experience appears to have been lacking among those who drafted Bill C-219. This has resulted in certain contradictions being built into the bill. As a prime example, the bill specifically directs the CDC to invest for profit in the best interests of the shareholders. I have no quarrel with that objective when it is applied to the broad spectrum of industrial investment opportunities, which the drafters of the bill presumably had in mind when drafting it. But the government, in my view, must make a clearer distinction than it has between general industrial investment and high risk, natural resource development investment.
If this distinction is not made, difficulties will eventually become inevitable. The specific directive contained in clause 6 stressing investments made both in anticipation of profit and in the best interests of the shareholders, while essential for general industrial investment, I am convinced will have an inhibiting effect on investment in risky, long-term mineral and hydrocarbon resource development. Once shares in the Canada Development Corporation are sold to the general public, it becomes inevitable that the directors will be concerned with the generation of revenue for the payment of dividends; and concentration upon investment areas of relatively low risk and certain ultimate yield to support dividend payments will occur. Mining and oil investment in particular are normally high risk. When this normally high risk is combined with the fact that Canada's major undiscovered and undeveloped hydrocarbon and mineral resources are in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, it is obvious that the risk is hardly compatible with regular dividend payments to shareholders.
Another section of the bill which 1 feel indicates the inattention of the drafters to mineral resource development is the one million dollar minimum which we find in clause 6 (2)(b). This provision reads:
-invest in the shares of corporations in each of which, in the opinion of the Board of Directors of the company, the real value of the shareholders' equity after investment by the company will be, or is likely to become, one million dollars or more.
In the mining field especially, it is quite likely that a number of extremely valuable investment opportunities will crop up from time to time, not necessarily restricted
Canada Development Corporation to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. However, let me concentrate attention upon these two areas. If the $1 million minimum remains it will rule out, or at least inhibit, management of the Canada Development Corporation taking steps to invest in some situations which in all probability, over a long period of time, will end up being an extremely good investment. I feel that this one million dollar minimum does not make very much sense, particularly as far as mining investment is concerned, though it may and probably does make sense when applied to the industrial and manufacturing spectrum.
While on the subject of resource development in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, may I say that it is in these regions that a development corporation is needed most and can contribute most to increasing the percentage of Canadian control over our mineral and hydrocarbon resources. In addition to the obvious economic advantages to Canada of CDC activity in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, such activity would give Canadians a more important sense of participation in national development and has the potential to be an important factor in this country's unity.
After all, 35 per cent of the Canadian land mass lies in the territories. Because its natural resources are under direct federal control, they are the common heritage of all Canadians and should be developed to the benefit of all Canadians, priority, of course, being given to ensuring that the needs of the residents of the northern territories are first met. Nevertheless, all Canadians have a direct stake in the resource development of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. For the CDC to give Canadians a sense of direct participation in the action in the northern territories would be an important contribution to national unity. This bill, with minor changes, combined with a wise selection of leadership for the CDC, has the potential of fulfilling the role I should like to see it play; but as it stands now, and with the emphasis of the bill where it is, I just do not think it will be able to play this role.
Another criticism that I have of this bill relates to the proposal to turn over Panarctic Oils Limited to the corporation at this time. Panarctic may take several more years and perhaps require hundreds of millions of dollars of additional investment before returns begin to flow back to its investors. Even with the tremendous capitalization proposed for the Canada Development Corporation, I doubt very much that the CDC would be prepared to continue to put in funds ranging conceivably to $100 million or more to protect the government's present 45 per cent interest in Panarctic. I, for one, would be extremely unhappy with, and totally opposed to, any reduction in the present 45 per cent interest of the federal government in Panarctic. I am convinced that in the long run this will turn out to be the best investment in Canada that the federal government has ever made. The Panarctic concept is one that I should like to see expanded into other areas, such as, conceivably, offshore hydrocarbon development and mineral development. I doubt very much whether even with its proposed capitalization the CDC would have the funds necessary to maintain a strong federal position in such possible investments.

March 3, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
I mentioned earlier that I thought the selection of the administrators of the CDC would be of prime importance. Certainly, if its chief officer has some mining and oil experience, or experience of resource development, then there will not be too much difficulty in convincing the CDC about resource development investment. But if we end up with a man at the top who has general manufacturing experience, it is inevitable that the CDC management will not put prime stress on resource development, which is where I feel it should be. I suggest to the minister a possible amendment which perhaps he will look at and discuss when the bill is referred to the committee. If we added powers under clause 7, by the addition of a subparagraph, permitting the establishment of a natural resources development company with all the powers of the Canada Development Corporation as outlined in clause 7, we would allow more flexibility.
I should like to see a subsidiary company set up by the Canada Development Corporation specifically designed to develop resources, with shares available to the public. It is absolutely essential that we distinguish between investment in general manufacturing and industrial enterprise across the country and investment in resource development. If shareholders require regular returns and dividends on their investment, we cannot combine this requirement with a daring and aggressive resources policy. Such a policy is essential if we are going to change the percentage of Canadian ownership and control in the resource industry.
We have a great natural resource potential. The CDC has the potential for ensuring a high degree of Canadian participation in the development of these natural resources, including the hydrocarbon industry. This is a painless way to accomplish a higher degree of Canadian control and ownership. We can do this without expropriating anything, and without nationalization. This can be accomplished by an aggressive pursuit of mineral and hydrocarbon investment by Canadians. Investment possibilities in this regard are now available in the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Finally, I should like to draw the minister's attention, and I am sure this has been done before, to the proposed take-over objective by Canada Development Corporation of the Northern Canada Power Corporation. How this matter got into the bill in the first place is difficult to understand. The Canada Development Corporation's expressed objective is to provide a profit for its shareholders. The objective of the Northern Canada Power Company is to provide electricity at cost to northern consumers. There is just no way these two objectives can exist side by side. The objective of the Northern Canada Power Company is not to make a profit for shareholders of the Canada Development Corporation at the expense of the users of electricity in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
If the minister has not already considered this, I urge him to take whatever steps are necessary to eliminate the reference to the NCPC. The two objectives are clearly irreconcilable. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary has
something to say in this regard. In terminating what I have to say on this subject, I again urge the minister to make a clear distinction, when the bill comes before the Committee, between general industrial development investment and natural resources investment.

subtopic: CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this debate in reference to Bill C-219. First of all, I should like to say that I concur with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). It is important that this bill be sent to the committee as quickly as possible in order that a number of matters which are of concern to a number of members in this House can be answered. While I am on my feet this afternoon, I should like to raise several questions and express my opinion. I hope the minister has made note of the various suggestions and will, at the appropriate time, make the appropriate reply.
Is there anyone in this House on the government side who can state the specific purpose of the proposed Canada Development Corporation? I ask that question with all sincerity in an endeavour to obtain a reasonable response. I have asked this question of members on the government side and members on this side. It appears that no one can clearly spell out the precise reason behind this legislation. It was my understanding that the Canada Development Corporation was being proposed to guarantee that certain Canadian interests which might be in danger of being taken over by foreign investors would be protected. I understand that this is not what the Canada Development Corporation is supposed to do.
I noted with some interest the press release of January 25 issued by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in which he attempted to spell out two or three reasons this legislation is necessary. It suggests that the bill provides for the establishment of a large corporation to do certain things, specifically to help develop and maintain Canadian control and Canadian management in the private sector. How can this be done? If one of the well established industries in the city of Toronto felt that its margin of profit over a given period of time did not warrant the continuation of its marginal operations and wanted to sell these operations to anyone who wished to purchase them, what could be done to keep these operations within the control of Canadians? If I managed such a company and I received a minimal offer, I would look elsewhere. I would run newspaper ads in the United States, and indeed in Europe, if I were interested in selling that company.
Then, if the CDC decided the retention of that company by Canadian interests was in the interests of Canada, it would have to be prepared to buy that company from the seller. Is it not conceivable that Canadians might feel that this company was worth, let us say, half a million dollars. An offer, indeed it could be a phony offer, might be made by United States interests in the amount of $750,000. Then, since the CDC had decided the retention of this industry in Canada was in the Canadian interest,

March 3, 1971

it would have to pay that higher price in order to retain it in Canada. I should like to know the type of companies the CDC will be interested in, how it intends to procure them and how it intends to convince the Canadian people that investment in these companies is a good idea. It is said that the CDC will provide greater opportunity for Canadians to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada. How will that be done? Will it be through the acquisition of companies, through the acquisition of shares or through the provision of risk capital to risk ventures?
I should like to have answers to some of these questions. For instance, we noted in the newspaper the other day the case of a plywood manufacturing company in Quebec which, after having been purchased by, I believe, the Quebec Development Corporation for something like $1,500,000 not too long ago, found it could not operate economically and is now being offered for sale for something like $500,000. Will the CDC pick up this plywood plant? If the CDC is indeed a profit-oriented corporation what right would it have to pick up that company? What I am a little suspicious about is it appears to me, so far as the Minister of Finance is concerned, that the CDC measure would seem to be a diversionary tactic to get the minds of the people off the more serious problem of unemployment. There seems to be an implied assurance to the people of Canada that they do not need to worry about being out of work because they will be given an opportunity to buy shares in a Canada development corporation, and in that way one day, will be rich.
I find it very difficult to conceive that the government would ask us to vote in favour of a measure which is so vague. Of course, vagueness is nothing new to this government, Mr. Speaker. We know from the hearings of the various committees that this is probably the most inept government in the history of Canada so far as the drafting of legislation is concerned. Thank God there is an opposition around to keep it on the straight and narrow. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance, who surely has some knowledge of business, who will determine the fair value of the four corporations that are to be purchased. I refer to Polymer Corporation Limited, Eldorado Nuclear Limited, Panarctic Oils Limited and Northern Transportation Company Limited. Are these conglomerates to become one entity when the CDC is in being? Who will sell these companies? I presume the government will sell them to the CDC. Who will determine the fair value of these companies and on what will the fair value be based? Will it be based on the performance record? Will it be based on earnings or potential earnings? What criteria is to be used when these companies are sold to the CDC? Will the price be so low that it will be embarrassing or will it be so high that profit will be impossible?
The minister says he is delighted to introduce this kind of a measure because, after all, it will give the Canadian people an opportunity to own shares in the CDC and in these companies. Does the minister not realize that now, although the people of Canada do not actually own the shares in these companies, they actually own the companies through their government. If the minister is right in
Canada Development Corporation
saying the CDC is profit-oriented, I wish him the best of luck in this endeavour. He says the CDC will not be a Crown corporation responsible to Parliament but will be a private corporation operating basically within the provisions of the Canada Corporations Act; but, because it is created by an act of Parliament any change in the capital structure, objects and powers of the corporation passed by the directors and shareholders will require approval by a resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament. Mr. Speaker, I ask who will exercise any degree of control over this corporation? Will it be the Minister of Finance or the Deputy Minister of Finance who will exercise majority control over this corporation?
Then, it is stated that, in addition to its broad powers of direct investment and participation in joint action with other Canadian investors, the CDC will be empowered to lend to other companies, guarantee their contracts and assist them in other ways. What does this mean? Carling's Brewery in Edmonton has found that the market has suffered a severe slump, as has been the case in almost every other market in recent months. They have found that Albertans do not drink as much beer as they should and their profits are down. Could they go to the CDC to borrow money and acquire assistance? Is this what the minister envisages? I do not know. I cannot quite understand it. At a time of unemployment and at a time when inflation is rampant, the government gives the impression of being concerned about the economic development of our country through the CDC. I am not certain it is an instrument of development. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance, who is a very dear friend of mine, whether he would agree with me on this point. I do not argue that it may not be in the government's best interest to create a corporation that would be in charge of the four companies to which I alluded earlier, but when we discuss the need for the private sector to gain access to risk capital, I should like to remind the minister that on the Prairies in particular when money is required for wildcat ventures-and the parliamentary secretary knows precisely to what I am referring-Canadians participate to a lesser extent than United States investors?
* (3:40 p.m.)
In this connection I could refer specifically to the various professions. It is odd that in Canada doctors, lawyers, engineers and wealthy businessmen would rather put their money into apartment houses, and thus be able to write off certain earnings, than put that money into risk ventures for the development of our natural resources. 1 suggest that the answer is very simple. If the minister changed the Canadian tax structure to allow the Canadian investor taking part in risk ventures the opportunity to write off certain losses over a given period of years there would be some incentive for such investment. If an investor who happened to make a bundle on a wildcat venture were taxed appropriately, and there is nothing wrong with that, that also would encourage risk investment. But it seems strange to me that the U.S. professional and businessman is more interested in gambling his capital in the resource development of western Can-

March 3, 1971
Canada Development Corporation ada than is the Canadian himself who really has an interest in that sort of development.
I say to the Minister of Finance in all sincerity that what he envisages for the CDC will ultimately turn out to be a bad dream. I think the direction in which we should be going at this point is to overhaul the tax structure as it is today.

subtopic: CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The issues raised by the proposed establishment of a Canada Development Corporation are significant. Therefore, this matter should be examined in detail by this House and by the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. In doing so, a complete survey should be made of the results of development corporations and their activities in other countries. It seems that we have a great penchant in Canada for adopting methods, procedures and policies that have proven to be not too successful in their lands of origin. We do not seem to learn from the experience of those countries.
It is important to be clear about the objectives of the suggested Canada Development Corporation. Although the absence of details makes appraisal dependent to a certain extent on inferences, it has been intimated that the CDC would primarily assist in the development of major projects in Canada and that it would seek to reduce foreign takeovers of Canadian enterprises. These objectives make all our hearts beat a little faster. Who could disapprove of the development of major projects by Canadians or the preservation of Canadian control of our industry? A development corporation can, of course, finance projects or curtail foreign ownership. An analysis of the costs involved and the consequences of this type of institution would demonstrate that this so-called solution may be self-defeating. Any projects that are economically viable would stand on their own feet, without government assistance.
I suggest that if the CDC were in evidence last fall, there would have been tremendous pressure on the government of Canada to take over Ryerson Press, pressures that probably would have proved irresistible. In considering this question I think it is well to reflect upon what the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and Information Canada could do with such an organization as Ryerson Press if it were under their control. I suggest that there would be a measure of control by the government of Canada if such an organization formed part of the holdings of CDC or anything like it.
The function of government is to give constructive help, in co-operation with the private sector, when a decision has been taken. Claims have been made that there is a large institutional gap in our capital market. What evidence is there for this assertion? One can think of all sorts of companies that have started from scratch in Canada recently, or alternatively large companies that have made substantial distributions of equity in Canada. We can think of the examples of Oshawa Wholesale, Couvrette, Alliance and the Bell Telephone Company.
But if this is so, it must also be admitted that there are large pools of capital lying around in savings accounts and certificates. The function of the government should be

to encourage the flow of these savings into active equity capital for the development of this country by Canadians. It could take positive steps such as giving a distinct tax advantage to Canadians for such investment instead of having them equal to or at a disadvantage in comparison with foreign investors. The government could also take steps to encourage provinces to reform their securities legislation for the protection of investors because, quite frankly, a great many people are frightened of the market, and I believe they are frightened with some cause. I would suggest also that if the provinces fail to co-operate in the enactment of uniform legislation, then consideration should be given to putting investor protection under federal jurisdiction.
As an answer to the problem of foreign ownership in Canada, a development corporation is a poor remedy. The free movement of capital, both across frontiers and domestically, should not be hindered by any government sponsored pool of capital. The Minister of Finance is confident that competent management would not make unrealistic bids to counter offers from foreign sources. For a foreign operating company with world wide outlets and unused plant facilities, the benefits of an amalgamation could justify a far higher price than any development corporation should pay. For instance, what would the CDC do with a national beer company?
The advantages of a Canadian outlet to a United States company are evident in that duplicate facilities are closed down and the production and sales forces are combined. Similarly, U.S. automobile manufacturers would have an incentive to acquire automobile parts companies in Canada, since parts used by the manufacturers of new cars can be moved across the borders duty free. It is difficult to see what a development corporation could do to check foreign ownership in most cases, apart from making an unrealistically high bid.
To counterbalance the objectionable consequences of foreign capital, legislation against the specific wrongs is the proper procedure. Whether it be Canadian dissatisfaction with the inadequate openings for Canadian talent, the lack of opportunity to participate in the processing of raw materials, the failure to compete in export markets, or merely inadequate adjustment to Canadian cultural patterns, it should manifest itself in specific legislation requiring foreign capital to conform to our requirements. By virtue of a favourable tax ruling, Rio Algom for example, was able to take over Atlas Steel advantageously. If the ruling had been changed either by a different interpretation or by legislation, this take over could have been thwarted.
If the Canadian Development Corporation were to develop major resources projects without outside participation, as has been suggested, in many cases sales outlets would be lacking. For example, United States or Japanese steel companies usually prefer to own their own raw material sources in order to ensure adequate supplies and also to participate in the profits of their own purchases, both being classical reasons for vertical integration. If Canada denied these opportunities to foreign steel companies, other nations would be more hospitable and as a nation we would be the losers.
March 3, 1971

In general, it is difficult to see how a Canada Development Corporation would invest its funds. Private pools of capital like the CED have not been able to invest all their available funds as it is. Even the Quebec General Investment Fund was not fully invested several years after it was started, and it is a relatively small fund, only a fraction of the size of the proposed CDC. Its dismal record augurs poorly for a Canada Development Corporation.
The Minister of Finance claims that the staff of a development corporation could be relatively immune from political intervention. There is almost no case of a government agency being able to withstand pressure from political sources. Even if the operating personnel were independent of day-to-day direction, the reality of government parentage would be an omnipresent fact. All but the most neurotic recognize and are influenced by their progenitors! A Canada Development Corporation would realize that if it incurred the displeasure of too many Members of Parliament or voters it would be abolished, something that is not true of most private enterprises. If a Canadian Development Corporation bought a large share in a foreign corporation with large operations in Canada in order to influence the Canadian operations, could one really trust the management to make decisions based on economic merit alone? It does not take a cynic to believe that the answer is a resounding no.
No reference has been made to Quebec, yet Quebec is one third of Canada and has already given notice that it wants to control new developments if possible. If the CDC performed managerial or entrepreneurial functions in addition to supplying capital the competent staff, which the Minister of Finance urges, would be spread over such a vast area of activities that supervision and detailed scrutiny could become a nightmare.
Reference has been made to our present emasculated form of equity ownership. Surely, all ownership in large corporations by outside shareholders must be at a distance unless that outside source sets itself up to be an expert and uses its position to get a seat on the board and dictate and change policy. Is this what the Canada Development Corporation will do? Will it be an expert in the mining, the pulp and paper, the utility and the oil business? Other countries, including the United Kingdom, have experimented with development corporations. We should remember the abortive groundnut scheme in Africa, which was promoted by a former British Labour government.
A few of the problems encountered by other development corporations of other countries can be summarized under a few general headings, the first of which is financing economically unsound enterprises. Social and political considerations frequently motivate development corporations. For example, the Chilean Development Corporation built steel mills that have proved to be high-cost and economically inefficient in Chile, and whose products have been unable to hurdle tariff barriers, particularly the 40 per cent Argentine surcharge on steel. In South Africa, the Industrial Corporation was established to
Canada Development Corporation
build an iron and steel complex, as well as facilities for obtaining oil from coal for strategic and military purposes. By that government's own admission, the government project displaced private investment and therefore negated its achievements.
Secondly, there is the question of inflation. Development corporations have built-in inflationary potential. Although funds may be supplied by individuals or private institutions, additional capital is often provided by the central bank or from foreign sources. When funds from private sources have not been forthcoming all too frequently development corporations have resorted to borrowing and rediscounting at the central bank, Also, once a program is under way its termination is difficult for political reasons.
The third problem is the displacement of private initiative and private capital. By their existence, development corporations absorb funds from abroad that would normally flow to private industry. Funds obtained from private domestic sources may be absorbed by the government development corporations, whereas under normal circumstances funds might seek their own investment outlets.
Fourth is the problem of excessive government control. In various countries development corporations have appointed directors to boards of businesses where their funds are invested. The IRI in Italy and the National Financiers of Mexico appoint directors of many companies. In general there could be a tendency to ignore the free forces of business in favour of political opportunism. For example, would the government permit the closing down of an unprofitable organization if thereby many people would lose their jobs?
The scope of action of the development corporation may become very wide, as in Burma where the initial step of the government in the 1950's was to set up a joint venture corporation of government and private businessmen. Most of Burma's imports then were bought by government organizations and the choice of suppliers was dictated by national agencies. In an attempt to diversify this economy by encouraging manufacturing, the government pursued a policy of state enterprise.
The fifth problem is that large enterprises may be favoured by the establishment of the Canada Development Corporation. In general, the special problems and risks of small enterprise financing have been a restraining factor. The careful investigation and supervision which this kind of financing necessitates makes it expensive. The number and variety of staff required to sift applications has meant that the large scale enterprises have often been the main beneficiaries of these development facilities, whereas the deserving small company has been neglected. The most successful government corporations in the economically advanced countries have been limited to specific and narrow areas of economic activity such as the transportation system, mortgages, or other credit institutions. Too frequently development corporations have very broad objectives which are difficult to accomplish.

March 3, 1971
Income Tax Act
The government should provide proper fiscal and monetary conditions for sound economic growth, combined with specific legislation to correct specific abuses that undoubtedly do occur. The CDC fails to come to grips with the problem of capital formation in Canada. Capital formation and development are the result of the savings process. Development corporations should be recognized as the reactionary and unworkable solutions that they are.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As the House is aware, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to implement two measures involving income tax changes of the several outlined in the budget that was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on December 3. One section of the bill will amend the Income Tax Act to make available a capital cost allowance supplement to manufacturing and processing industries. The other section of the bill will amend Chapter 38 of the Statutes of Canada 1967-68 to provide for an extension of the income surtax on
individuals and corporations from the end of 1970 to the end of 1971.
To encourage increased capital investment in manufacturing and processing, which recently has been relatively weak, the bill provides that those engaged in such businesses may claim capital cost allowance for 115 per cent of the actual cost of machinery, equipment and structures acquired between December 4, 1970, and March 31, 1972. The effect of this measure is to enable a qualifying taxpayer to claim capital cost allowance over a period of years of $115 for every $100 of actual capital investment put in place, an increase of $15 over the amount that normally could be written off against earnings.
It is estimated that manufacturing and processing enterprises undertake some $3 billion worth of capital investment annually that would qualify for this special allowance. Investment of this order therefore, would enable these enterprises to claim an extra capital allowance over the depreciable lifetime of assets put in place within the period up to March, 1972, of around $450 million. While the cost to the treasury of this measure is estimated at $25 million for the 1971-72 fiscal year, the cumulative capital cost allowance benefits being provided to manufacturing and processing businesses over a period of years will provide a significant stimulus to increased investment in these two sectors over the next several months.
I might mention that the definition of a manufacturing or processing business and the description of assets qualifying for the supplementary allowance will be contained in regulations to be adopted soon after approval of the legislation. It is proposed, however, that the definition of a qualifying business would be very similar to that now found in class 19 of the Income Tax Regulations, while the property that would qualify would be buildings as described in class 3 or 6 and machinery and equipment that is normally included in class 8 of schedule B of the same regulations.
The second section of the bill before the House extends for a further year the 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporate income. Members will recall that this surtax on individuals does not apply to the first $200 of basic tax, with the result that more than 25 per cent of Canadian taxpayers will continue to be exempted from payment of the additional levy. No surtax is paid by a single person whose income is below $2,743, nor by a married man with two children whose income is below $4,343.
I would be less than frank, Mr. Speaker, if I did not acknowledge that the decision reluctantly reached by the government to extend the surtax to the end of 1971 was a source of disappointment to many taxpayers. It was also a source of some criticism, frequently from those who were unaware of or did not understand the considerations which led the government to the conclusion that this was the best course to follow in the long term interests of the nation as a whole.

March 3, 1971

In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance made it clear that the government reached the conclusion late last year that it was appropriate to provide an additional stimulus to the economy in order to reinforce the series of expansionary fiscal and monetary measures adopted since the early months of 1970.
Having reached that conclusion, the government was faced with the need to reach a decision on two important questions. It had to decide how much additional stimulus could safely be injected into the economy without running an excessive risk of creating new inflationary pressures in the months ahead. Then it had to decide what form this additional stimulus should take in order to provide the maximum possible assistance in the shortest possible time to individuals, regions and industries in Canada most adversely affected by slow growth of the economy.
In reaching a judgment on the first question, the government had to consider how far it could go in creating additional fiscal stimulus by adding to its cash requirements without imposing dangerous pressures on Canada's monetary system. As the Minister of Finance noted in his budget speech:
There are limits to the extent to which the banks can be encouraged to increase their holdings of government securities without running the very serious risk that the expansion and increased liquidity of the banking system will trigger inflation and expectations of inflation.
This very fundamental point was also underlined by the Economic Council of Canada in its most recent review of the economy. "Monetary policy (together with fiscal policy with which it is closely interrelated)," the council emphasized, "should evolve in a way that seeks to avoid large destabilizing swings in the growth of the money supply." Even the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) appeared to recognize that there are some very real limits on the extent to which the government can reasonably expand fiscal policy when he noted during the budget debate that the government faced "a substantial and increasing budgetary deficit" as a result of the expansionary policies which it has adopted. That recognition, however, has not deterred either the Conservative leader or other members opposite from advocating measures that would enlarge the budgetary deficit and the government's cash requirements in a massive way.
In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance estimated the government would have cash requirements during the current fiscal year of around $1.57 billion, excluding those for foreign exchange reserves. This represents a massive swing of more than $1.7 billion from the position in 1969-70 and is a measure of the very large stimulus injected into the economy in the current fiscal year by the government. For 1971-72, the minister estimated the government's cash requirements would rise to $1.9 billion, matching the record peacetime level of 1968-69 and representing a swing of more than $2.1 billion from the level in the last fiscal year.
The second question facing the government was whether additional stimulus of this degree should be provided through increased spending and lending, through a
Income Tax Act
decrease in taxes, or a combination of the two. There have been suggestions from some quarters that the government decided against allowing the surtax to expire and perhaps further reducing taxes as well because of a mistaken belief that reducing taxes would be inflationary. Nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker.
The fact is, as the Minister of Finance indicated in his budget, that the government concluded it would be considerably more appropriate in the economic circumstances facing the nation to adopt increased spending and lending programs aimed at providing early and direct assistance and support to individuals, regions and industries most in need of it, rather than to provide additional stimulus by means of a tax cut that would provide greatest benefit to the more prosperous sectors of the economy.
It should be pointed out, however, that while these selective measures will have their most immediate and direct impact on the economically weaker sector of the economy, they will also provide a stimulus to the economy as a whole by reinforcing the upward thrust being provided by the parallel expansion of monetary policy that has been under way since early in 1970.
The special capital cost allowance supplement being provided in the bill now before the House for capital investment undertaken by manufacturing and processing industries is one of those selective measures adopted by the government to provide a significant boost to a sector of the economy that has been particularly slack recently.
The decision to propose extension of the income surtax to the end of the current year, which is provided for in the second section of the bill, was reached by the government with considerable reluctance but with the strong conviction that such action was necessary in the best interests of the nation as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, this particular part of the extended budget debate appears to be anticlimatic in that it is almost three months since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) delivered his budget message and indicated that there would be these two tax changes. I find it rather strange, looking at the continuation of the surtax which, of course, had a very dubious parentage. It was a misconception to start with and eventually a miscarriage.
It was finally brought in at the three per cent level. We have seen it extended, although we find singularly regrettable the words of the parliamentary secretary and the Minister of Finance that they were beginning their monetary expansion policy early in 1970. It is true that in the June or late May budget, they dropped the idea of a three per cent sales tax. I suppose it was anticipated at that time that the changes in the white paper on taxation would have been reported upon and brought into this House, allowing the government to bring in the tax changes and incorporate the three per cent surcharge into the ordinary tax rate. This was fully the intention of the government.

In June the Minister of Finance indicated that he was going to allow the surcharge to die as of December 31, as it was not being renewed in the June budget. We also know it had been the intention not to present a budget, until the very last moment, for other than fiscal and monetary reasons, a budget was presented in order to sweeten the pot. It was a very feeble gesture because it was all promises for the future, not for this winter, arising out of the troubles of last autumn. That is what it was. Let's call a spade a spade.
The budget was one of the government's ways of reacting to the October crisis in the province of Quebec. It was also its belated recognition of the problem of unemployment, particularly in the Atlantic region and the province of Quebec. After all, the budget did not do anything for the other provinces. The parliamentary secretary shakes his head and purses his lips. The loan fund of $150 million or $160 million is supposed to be the anchor of this budget. It provides precisely $1.6 million for the entire province of Alberta for the end of fiscal 1970-71. Why, a spit in the ocean would do more than that to deal with the problem.
Many of the other things that are going to happen will only happen in the spring or after March 31. They may happen during May or June. If this was supposed to be a budget to alleviate winter unemployment across Canada, I say it was a complete and utter hoax. That is why it was so empty. The Minister of Finance can always use an extra couple of hundred million dollars. This government operates on the basis that you have to raise the money because you have the expenditures. Expenditures are already going up to approximately $15 billion. The government always taxes up to its expenditures.
If the government wanted to be careful in their expenditures in many sectors, there would not be this necessity for ever increasing demands upon the economy, far in excess of what the economy can stand. The sins are not entirely those of this particular administration, although the ministry must share the responsibility because most of them were members of the previous ministry which embarked upon programs which went beyond any rhyme or reason when measured against the economy.
If one had to put a cost benefit analysis on the economy and the spending programs, the programs would have been out the window long before this. But, no, it seemed to be politically expedient to establish certain programs and to blazes with the expense and damn the torpedoes. There they are. We are now receiving the bills. These are getting higher and higher all the time.
I wish to deal with the two particular items of this bill. They epitomize, in actual fact, the schizophrenia of the government when it comes to its monetary and fiscal policies. On the monetary side, we are told that the government is increasing the pace of the relaxation of restrictions to get the economy moving again. There were certain changes with regard to monetary policy starting in the spring. But of all the stupid things, that had to be the one. Even more paradoxical, in the June budget there were to be some retail sales credit restrictions which, of course, were never implemented because somebody finally saw the light. I do not know who it was, but they were proven to be extremely obtuse about these matters and insisted even into July that the regulations were being formulated. Then, of course, came the dawn. Unemployment was very serious. The government decided to drop the retail sales credit restrictions. This was one of the gestures given to the country. It would never have worked, and would only have increased unemployment.
It is remarkable as to how this surtax has changed over the past three years. It was imposed at the time of the monetary crisis in 1967-68. It was to be a dampener on the economy. It was renewed in 1969 because inflation was very pressing. The surtax had to be continued and extended to the end of 1970. In December, 1970, when employment was the number one problem and, to use the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), inflation had been licked, we were asked to continue the three per cent surtax. What is it now? Is it anti-inflationary? Inflation was supposed to have been beaten and controlled. Now, it is incorporated into the normal tax framework and will continue to be part of the anticipated revenues to be raised by the government. In other words, it is no longer a surtax; it becomes part and parcel of the normal tax structure. Moreover, the fact is that it is inflationary rather than anti-inflationary. The imposition of a surtax of this kind in a day and age when tax is deducted at source from the majority of working people means simply that in the next round of wage increases the cost of the surcharge is passed on to the employer. It is the take-home pay that counts. As far as the three per cent surcharge on corporate incomes is concerned, it is soon fed through the price structure back to the consumer. I would have thought this was so apparent to everyone that the government would have refused to resort to such a device. As a matter of fact, the government has been fighting inflation with the wrong weapons for far too long. As a result, we find ourselves in a serious depression.
By what means does the government intend to combat the recession? Not with a really expansionary budget. The one feature which the minister produced with regard to income tax changes involved a 15 per cent premium or bonus in connection with capital cost allowances. This looks very well on paper but it is difficult to foretell the result or the cost to the economy. Actually, this concession will cost the government nothing. As a result of the expansion which will be made in anticipation of this 15 per cent allowance, there will be increases in receipts from sales tax and additional benefits accruing to the treasury. So, on a net basis any loss will be more than made up by additional tax revenue from various sources. As I say, it is difficult to estimate what the total cost will be. Nevertheless, this is the type of tax incentive of which I tend to approve. All I can say is that on the basis of what we know today it is difficult to understand precisely the type of expenditure to which this concession will apply. Some elaboration will be required on the part of the parliamentary secretary when he replies.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand the provisions of the bill now before the House, the loss of revenue to the government as a result of provisions in one portion of the bill will be roughly equal to the gain in revenue achieved by the application of provisions in another portion of the bill. This brings to my mind the Biblical quotation: "The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away. Blessed be the name of the Lord". I suppose the 1971 version of this Biblical quotation might be: "The minister giveth and the minister taketh away. Blessed be the name of the Prime Minister".
Hear, hear!

If hon. members are happy with that, that is fine.
This bill extends the application of the 3 per cent surcharge on income tax. The relevant section of the act will now read as follows:
This section is applicable to taxation years commencing or ending in or coinciding with 1968, 1969, 1970 or 1971-
It is almost beginning to read like a litany. This is now the third time we have had this surtax extended or reintroduced in the House of Commons.
To my mind, nothing can better illustrate the Liberal record of fiscal bungling and mismanagement than the story involved in this bill and the history of this particular tax measure. It seems that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is a man who can use an argument to suit every occasion. When I was preparing for this debate I had occasion to take a look at what the minister said in 1969, at which time he made it very clear that the government was not introducing the bill for purposes of revenue. At that time, the bill extended this particular surtax into 1969 and 1970, the measure having first been announced in the budget speech on June 3. The minister, however, did not get around to introducing the measure until some time late in the fall, and it was debated in December 1969. When the minister announced the extension of this surtax on June 3, he said it would be clear to

everybody that an extension of the surtax at that time was required for the purpose of economic stabilization and not for budgetary revenues.

By the time the minister got around to introducing the bill in the House of Commons the situation had changed. In June of 1969 when the minister first announced the institution of the surtax he pointed out that there were a number of factors which led the government to make this decision. He said the economy had demonstrated a strong performance at that time and that prices were continuing to climb. He said there were strong international pressures. By the time the minister introduced the bill, that situation no longer prevailed. In any event he barrelled straight ahead with the institution of a surtax, regardless of the fact that he was dealing with a different situation, and applied the measure announced in the middle of 1969.
This time the minister has a different reason for continuing the surtax. He made it quite clear in his budget address of December 3, 1970, that cash requirements represented the basic reason for extending the surtax. He said that in adopting this policy the government had decided that this would add greatly to its cash position. He went on to deal with a number of factors, one of which was the pressure for extra cash, which led the government to decide to extend the surtax into 1971. Who pays for this? Of course, the Canadian taxpayer must pay.
We have heard the Minister of Finance make other statements in the House dealing with this particular matter which are contrary and conflicting. I think for a moment we should refer again to the budget speech delivered on the night of December 3 last. At that time, the Minister of Finance was presenting a financial statement to the House of Commons. There were expectations that he would provide some stimulus to the Canadian economy. Unfortunately, there was nothing of the sort. I suggest that the best stimulus the minister could have provided to the economy at that time was a tax cut. This should have included a provision whereby this surtax would have been allowed to lapse at the end of 1970 rather than, as envisaged by the present legislation, being extended throughout 1971.
I want to make it clear that we in the NDP feel that further relief is needed through a tax credit system. This would assist our economy. I find it very difficult to understand why the minister did not respond to the situation that existed in December. It was perfectly clear then, to anyone who was prepared to analyze the situation and see what was ahead of us, that we were approaching a period of depression or recession, whatever you like to call it. Our unemployment rate was increasing at a terrible pace. Every indication was that the recovery of our economy would be very slow in 1971, and that in the meantime there would be no appreciable pick-up in economic activity. It was apparent from the early part of 1971 that there would be a relatively slow increase in he economic activity. This was the projection at that time.
