There has been nothing to indicate there has been any change in the situation.
The minister stated in his remarks that anyone with an income of less than $2,743 would not be affected by the extension of this surtax. Of course, this is correct. I am sure there will be a greater number of people than in previous years who will not be affected by this extension of the surtax because of the unemployment situation. I am sure that a great many of the 668,000 people, who were reported to be out of work in the middle of January, will not have any worry about the extension of this surtax, because their incomes will be reduced as a result of the slowdown of economic activity.
It is difficult to understand why the government, which is responsible for the over-all direction and management of the economy of this nation, did not provide greater stimulus. The answer can only be found when we consider the points raised on a number of occasions by many members of this House regarding the government's policy in respect of taxation. The government is looking at a different sort of schedule, one which does not involve merely an improvement in the rate of economic activity in 1971. There is something else involved. I suggest that "something else" is an election schedule, and the events leading up to the government's plan for an election.
There is no doubt that the government is planning for an election in mid-1972. I am sure there are many who feel that if we allow the economy to pick up too quickly in 1971,-by the time we reach the middle of 1972, people will not remember this unemployment situation. Thus, it is much better to stall off for a good portion of 1971, allowing the economic pick-up to take place toward the end of this year. According to this sort of reasoning, by the middle of 1972 the Canadian economy will be rolling fine, and things will be in good shape for the Liberal party to call a federal election. I suggest that a tax cut announced in the budget of December 3 would have been a real stimulus to the Canadian economy. It would have been of great help and might have had some beneficial effect on the rate of unemployment we are experiencing at this present moment. The government chose to do otherwise.
I should like to turn back for a few minutes to review some of the sordid history of this surtax, which really is very strange and unusual. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out, it was on November 30, 1967 that the then Minister of Finance, who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) announced this tax in his budget statement:
I come now to my tax proposals. My first proposal relates to the personal income tax. I am asking the house to approve a special surtax of 5 per cent of the amount of the basic tax assessed on an individual in excess of $100. This surtax will take effect January 1st and would remain I expect until we have completed the transition to a slower rate of growth of expenditures or until economic and financial conditions call for a change in our fiscal policy.
That was the statement in which the then Minister of Finance announced this particular measure. The resolution was introduced in the House of Commons on December 14,	1967, and the bill was introduced on
Income Tax Act
February 6, 1968. It came up for second reading, at which time the then Minister of Finance made certain remarks. Then, something happened. I am sure this must still make hon. members on the government side of the House shudder. On February 19, 1968, the government bill was defeated by a vote of 84 to 82. This was a clear indication of a lack of confidence in the government. Nevertheless, the government managed to survive this situation.
They must have had some second thoughts because it was announced that the then Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, was to retire and that a Liberal Leadership Convention would be held. I am sure at that time the Liberals must have thought that after the leadership convention they would want to hold an election, and that it would be much better to have a different type of tax measure before the House of Commons than that which had been first proposed and defeated in the House. So, finally a new bill was presented on March 7, 1968 which was not quite as bad as the original measure. However, it ran into some procedural difficulty and another bill was introduced on March 12, 1968. At that time the Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, made a very lengthy speech in which he defended the government's record and pointed to the necessity for fiscal restraint. He used this as a defence in respect of introducing the surtax at that time. He went on to quote various authorities to back up his statement that this measure was needed in the interests of fiscal restraint and because of the necessity to slow down the economy.
What is the situation now? I think this was pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Skoreyko). Are we dealing with an inflationary situation? Is there no need to stimulate the economy and encourage economic activity? Are the government's policies adequate to deal with the present level of unemployment? I suggest the government's economic policies have been found to be totally lacking. This was pointed out to the government this week when the Canadian Labour Congress presented its brief to the federal cabinet. There were some pretty strong words used by the Canadian Labour Congress in its brief, and rightly so. I notice the parliamentary secretary smiles when I refer to this particular brief. I do not think some of the government's ministers were smiling when they listened to the words used by the Canadian Labour Congress, because that organization was speaking on behalf of many of the 668,000 people who are out of work, according to the January statistics. That figure probably is higher now.
In its brief, the CLC stated:
What disturbs us, and many others, is that our current unemployment problem has been artificially created. It is not the result of natural business recessionary conditions. It is the direct result of coldly-calculated policies whose sole object was to induce unemployment in order to combat inflation. Your government's anti-inflationary program, based for a long time on very tight fiscal and monetary policies, has been primarily responsible for the fact that we have hundreds of thousands of unemployed Canadians. Your government's strict adherence to "conventional economic wisdom" in attempting to deal with an

Then, the brief stated further:
Never before in the history of this country did a Prime Minister state before a national audience that it was his government's intent to allow unemployment to rise ''if necessary to 6 per cent", to combat inflation. Now, Mr. Speaker, the other section of this bill, of course, deals with capital cost allowances. This matter has already been referred to in the introductory remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney), as well as by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). Of course, we know that in the manufacturing and processing industries owners of depreciable assets put in place between December 4, 1970 and March 31, 1972 will be able to write-off 115 per cent of the original cost according to the government's proposal.
The government, through this measure, intends to stimulate private investment and the economy. There are three different approaches to illustrate the stimulating effect these proposals which have been advanced are planned to have on private investment. The first suggestion is that 7.5 per cent of the cost of the asset will be added to earnings over the depreciable life of the asset. Second, it could be viewed as a 6 per cent reduction in the effective cost of the machinery according to calculations by Clarkson Gordon. Third, it could be viewed as having the same effect as about a 3 per cent reduction in interest rates the first year. There are really two important consequences which arise out of this which should be noted. The first is that businessmen could accelerate their investment plans or proceed with investment plans that had previously been marginal, both in order to take advantage of the more generous allowance being proposed. Secondly, businessmen who had already made investment plans will receive a windfall gain.
When we attempt to evaluate the government's proposal to increase capital cost allowances, I think one must ask what economic goals the proposal is intended to achieve and how effective the proposal will be in achieving them. The budget address of the Minister of Finance on December 3 last purported to set down in a concise
manner the economic strategy of the government for achieving our first economic objective, a steady and sustainable improvement in the real income of Canadians everywhere. Then, later on in the budget speech, the minister stated that a steady and sustainable improvement in the standard of living of all Canadians requires the fullest possible utilization of the nation's human and material resources. This really means full employment. In addition to full employment the speech indicates that economic stability, a good price and cost performance and a satisfactory balance of payments are necessary pre-conditions to the economic goals.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance also stated that the latest figures on capital investment, apart from housing, are also stronger and that the recent preliminary survey of capital investment intentions indicates growing strength in this area of activity next year. Activity in this sector this year has been one of the weaker elements in the economy. Later on in the budget address the Minister of Finance noted that private capital investment has been one of the weaker elements in the investment picture, particularly investment in secondary industries. He went on to describe this measure as an example of selective fiscal policy since it applies only to the manufacturing and processing industry. The result, he predicts, will be new capital projects, a speed up in the outlays planned for the future, all leading to new jobs for a variety of skilled people in the labour force.
The DBS survey of capital spending intentions for the 200 largest companies in Canada indicates an 11 per cent increase in 1971. This survey of course was taken before the Minister of Finance presented his budget statement. However, the increases in the manufacturing sector are expected to be more moderate. The Economic Council of Canada, in its medium term capital investment survey, projects about a 9 per cent increase in 1971 for all industries, and some 6.2 per cent in the manufacturing sector. However, the subsectors of manufacturing show a wide diversity of intentions. For food and beverages, it is an increase of 1.2 per cent; for pulp and paper, a drop of 11.9 per cent; for primary metals, an increase of 40.8 per cent; for chemicals, an increase of only 11.4 per cent; for transportation equipment, a drop of 36.6 per cent; and for others, an increase of 15.7 per cent.
The figures for the subsectors of the manufacturing industry indicate that perhaps the capital cost allowance proposal was not selective enough. The primary metal industry, which already had planned a 40 per cent increase in capital expenditures, will receive a substantial windfall gain. The pulp and paper industry on the other hand, which has excess capacity and which brings the average investment intentions for manufacturing down, will probably not be taking advantage of the proposal. Where, on the one hand, the application of the increased capital cost allowance proposal may be too broad, the restriction on the type of expenditures that are eligible may be too narrow. Research and development expenditures, and expenditures on pollution abatement, are examples of the type of capital investment that

are not eligible in many respects. Since 11 per cent of the capital investment intentions of the pulp and paper firms surveyed were directed toward pollution abatement expenditures, how much of this would be new plant equipment which would qualify under this proposal?

Ottawa's policy makers are counting heavily on the budget's extra write off to spark new capital investment in 1971-but so far industry is reacting coolly to the incentive.
Finance Department officials told Financial Post they expect that the rise in capital cost allowances to 115 per cent will have the biggest economic impact of the various measures proposed.
Industry-to judge by an FP roundup of opinion this week

thinks the incentive will provide "only minor stimulus'' to industrial expansion.
That is the view of most makers of pulp and paper, food equipment, plastics, steel, computers and other products canvassed by FP. Only a few companies said Benson's proposal might have any effect on their expansion plans.
The Financial Post went on to note the regional implications of this proposal, which leave something to be desired. The article then continues:
Those skeptical of the scheme's pull point out that Benson's proposal is not likely to be as powerful a stimulus as other measures in the 1960s, such as the U.S. 7 per cent investment tax credit or various fast write-offs made available by the 1962-64 budgets of Walter Gordon.
What's more, it's claimed by critics, the value of the extra capital cost allowance will be obscured by continuation of the 3 per cent tax surcharge.
Later on the article points out some of the reasons this particular measure would not have the desired effect for those sectors of the economy in which it was desired to bring about expansion. The article reads:
But design, land, purchase, and other preliminary activity would take about a year and a half. Construction could probably only be started when Benson's program was ending.
Ironically, companies that had already made expansion decisions but had not yet received machinery or equipment, or taken possession of new buildings, will receive an unexpected windfall.
Conversely, companies that make the decision to expand during the 16 months of the program, but leave it too late to take delivery before March 31, 1972, will lose out.
This should mean, for most practical purposes, that management expansion decisions will have to be taken during the first half of 1971 in most cases in order to qualify. And that is exactly what Ottawa wants to see happen.
But of course, it was pointed out in the article that this is not likely to take place to nearly the extent that is anticipated by the Department of Finance. Thus we see that this measure will not have nearly the stimulating effect on the Canadian economy that the government has anticipated and that it had hoped for in making the announcement that it did on December 3.

The report to the tax authorities can understate actual earnings to a degree that is totally misleading of their value. Would the trend have declined so vigorously (if at all) last year if corporations hadn't been writing off new investment of the preceding years at, the maximum rates?
Later, the article continues:
This is one major cause for another look at capital cost allowances. Another is the consequences for the company that makes maximum use of them.
The article goes on to deal further with the subject. This shows that the minister himself, has, on various occasions in the past, expressed a great deal of doubt about the value of this particular mechanism in stimulating the economy. It can have inevitable and undesirable consequences for the economy as a whole. Thus, I feel that this is the worst possible kind of bill. It demonstrates Liberal incompetence and their callousness toward the needs of Canadian people. Consequently, we in this party will oppose the bill to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker. I am happy to say a few words about Bill C-225 extending for another year the so-called 3 per cent social development tax.
When the government levied that surtax, it was just to offset an apparent deficit and for one year only. It is now in its third year and this will be the third extension of its duration.
The last budget reveals that in Canada debt service has increased by some $2 billion within the last few decades, and the population of Canada is increasingly living in poverty.
Indeed, Canadians are living in abject poverty and this fact is recognized by all. There is no end to the expenses involved in setting up commissions which are instructed to determine whether there are poor people in Canada, how many of them there are, and how to deal with the problem.

But with an increase in taxes and the continuation of the 3 per cent surtax, Canadian citizens will have to pay these taxes and thus our taxpayers will lose the purchasing power which they had of could have had.
Then why is the government continuing this tax while we of the Ralliement Creditiste are advocating the introduction of a federal measure to establish an integrated credit for the whole of Canada. Accordingly, we tell the government that this economic monetary dictatorship is at the root of all our evils, of all our economic and social problems. We want a provincial and a federal legislation to wage war against poverty.
Will the extension of this 3 per cent surtax enable the government to achieve the stated aims? Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with an unpleasant and unfair situation just as we are pressing for a just legislation in a united Canada.
So, there is something the matter. What is preventing discussion and knowing the reason for the extension of this tax? To know it, you have to examine the meanders of the financial system.
According to the increase in taxes we have, or to the extension of this tax, our fiscal system is unfair. I will say that those who proclaim it, as well as those who accept it, are accessories to injustice and social disorder, accessories to anarchy, responsible for the present unbalance, responsible for taxes and surtaxes of all kinds, responsible for debts, for public and collective debts, since the extension of this tax will increase further collective debts and public debts, and even private debts. They are therefore responsible for poverty in families, responsible for dread, fear and all unnecessary privations.
The economy as advocated by the government is responsible and unfair, and is part of the injustice suffered by many Canadians. Our whole taxation system is the result of a financial system built on injustices. Our system is the aggregate of finance companies that control the financial system. It is a para-international system. Banks issue currencies that we call credit based on the real wealth of the country. Very well. Without that, credit would be valueless, because it constitutes the real wealth. Then, the credit money is only a symbol of real wealth. The true wealth is the thing; money is the symbol based on the thing. Therefore, it is recognized that credit given by various institutions is based on the true wealth of the country, that belongs to the country, that is is inhabitants.
As a matter of fact, there is individual wealth and collective wealth. Our financial associations or bodies are only individuals amongst other individuals; they are responsible for the money of the country, and now they proclaim themselves the owners of the money issued by them, as soon as it is issued; the owners of credit in order to cancel it when they decide to do so; the absolute owners of all the circulating currency, since they appoint themselves masters of the birth and death of money.
The extension of this tax, Mr. Speaker, is necessarily a reflection of wealth. The banks claim for themselves the ownership of money. Wealth is owned by citizens, but
money, the symbol of wealth, is unjustly recognized as the property of bankers. With money, bankers have in their hands the tool necessary to take over all the wealth; they have taken over a good part of it. This is one of the reasons why the government was obliged to extend these taxes.
The financial institutions hold a mortgage on all real wealth, both public and private. The total debt of the country which comprises both private and public debts outweighs considerably the value of such weal.h. The total debt of the country is the credit of the financiers. Banks own indirectly all the wealth of Canada and of Canadians; they claim an interest on these riches, and they may at any time demand the repayment of the capital. They can seize the capital whenever they like. The debts of the country to the financiers prove that this system is unfair and antisocial.
We find ourselves again in a tragic situation: either taxes are increased or the 3 per cent surtax continues to be in effect.
The present taxes are not necessary for the common good because they are levied only to pay interests to a few privileged institutions, to a few individuals who have the right of life or death over the institutions, the companies, the citizens, the government, and who thus become deprived, frustrated of their first and vital necessity. Those taxes merely and simply become a theft. They are part of a strategy organized by the powerful to strengthen their own power and, at the same time, weaken the power of individuals, of governments, who are right in claiming the ownership of the actual wealth which they create by their work.
Thus theft goes with tyranny. We must at all costs change this financial system, since the riches of the world were created for all men. It is the duty of Parliament to put them at the service of men, under the control of this government. All citizens must be able to enjoy a fair share of those riches made available to them by nature and industry and the extension of this tax does exactly the opposite.
Workers in this country create wealth and our financial institutions do the accounting so as to enable the citizens to exchange that wealth. That accounting is money. The Canadian people are by right the owners of that wealth and our institutions are constituting themselves owners of the money they make. Therefore our institutions, through a simple accounting process, register to their own credit what should be the assets of this country and at the same time they wish to register as national liabilities all the riches of this country. That last operation is practised when banks or financial institutions enter as the borrowers' liabilities, who are individuals and governments, that credit based upon riches. Financiers can steal that way because the money they create is created in the form of loans to individuals and of bonds. All the money that is made and thus created by the banks, as debts, is debt money.
The more people are taxed, the more taxes are increased and the more the people are buried in misery and austerity.

Financial institutions lend money but do not lend interest. They demand the repayment of those loans plus the interest they did not create. Such is the nonsense of that system that is becoming the greatest fraud in history.
The national debt means the national resources that were stolen by those institutions. At the present time, we keep increasing the nation's debt and pushing our people deeper into economic stagnation, for 25 per cent of our budget goes for social welfare, whereas 14 per cent of it is used for economic support and expansion. This means that social welfare institutions gobble up almost three quarters of our budget. When a country has reached the point where it devotes that much of its budget to keep people from starving to death, to pay unemployment benefits and social welfare allowances to the poor, an increase in taxes is surely untimely. This is no time to extend the application of taxes.
We must, as members of Parliament, vote against this tax and abolish it as soon as possible and reduce the debenture rate. When government bonds are sold instead of buying them back at the new interest rate of 7, 8 or 9 per cent, we should at least keep the rate at its previous level. This would be doing something for the people. As long as we fail to do that, we shall keep on increasing debts, taxes, unemployment and public welfare costs.
This leads us to blame severely the government and the opposition for not opening their eyes in time to bring the necessary changes that would allow Canada to progress and live in affluence. Instead of distributing scarcity, of increasing taxes and of giving piecemeal to our citizens what they are entitled to have, we could give them directly everything they need and we would still be able to administer within our system, because the capitalist system is the best in the world.
We are faced with two ideologies: the communist ideology and the capitalist ideology.
If we are unable to come up with a better and more humane ideology, I wonder where we will end up.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-225, which is a small measure introduced to change the tax law, I must first say that I think it is small in scope but large in result. It indicates the way in which the government is carrying out its course of action for the economic and fiscal well-being of Canada.
The state of the Canadian economy is not all that good. We have one of the highest unemployment rates in the western world. Dr. O. J. Firestone, who was one of Ottawa's most powerful bureaucrats of a decade ago, recently wrote an article for the Canadian Tax Journal. He had a lot to say, nearly all bad, about this administration's anti-inflationary policy.
He writes:
The question is not whether the Canadian government should have pursued anti-inflationary policies. Rather the question is whether it was necessary to go so far out of line with the economic performance of most of the industrialized countries of the world.
Compared with the other 18 so-called OECD countries, we have created in Canada the highest level of unemployment among the industrialized nations. Consumer prices are lower admittedly than in most of the OECD countries, but in terms of industrial production we have the fourth worst record of OECD countries. Dr. Firestone estimates that a more lenient application of policies to control inflation could have increased the gross national product by $2 billion and found 200,000 new jobs.
Dr. Firestone goes on to say:
Did Canada pay too high a price in becoming the world's leading nation in fighting inflation?
He predicts there will be "continuing under-utilization of the nation's production capacity" for 1972 as well as this year. It is indeed a grim assessment of a government which has hired all sorts of experts to help it with the management of the nation's business.
Canada may have had the greatest measure of price stability in the western world, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has stated, but it also has had the highest level of unemployment with a consequent loss of close to $2 billion in gross national product. Nor have there been any indications of material changes this year in spite of the government's effort at pump priming, in the main through regional development incentives. Indeed, it is unlikely to show any improvement on last year's 3 per cent. A large part of the reason for this is that the government has drained the well of private productivity. Inflation has taken its toll of private productivity and high taxes and labour costs have also lowered the well.
The profitability of business-still the largest source of employment-has been declining since 1965-66 in spite of the physical growth that has been attained. Attempts by the government to take up the slack have not been too

successful. The cost of job creation in the government section is considerably greater than in the private sector. And in this manner, Mr. Speaker, I think that a tax reduction would be indicated and it is for this reason that I oppose the retention of the three per cent surtax.
The white paper proposal for tax reforms based on 1969 income would extract an estimated $205 million in its first year and $560 million in its fifth year. We cannot forecast what effect the white paper on taxation will have on the flow into financing growth. I do not think that anyone seriously questions that savings will be diverted.
Then, there is the high unemployment benefits, higher pensions and related measures. All are very desirable, but all pre-empt funds from business growth. In the past some of these funds came from outside the country. However, these will likely be reduced in the future. They are being repelled by high taxation and uncertainty. It seems that the government is basically in contradiction with itself. It is increasing its demand on domestic funds when it should be reducing them. I oppose the retention of the 3 per cent surtax at this time, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, there is now before the House a government motion designed to extend the so-called social development tax of 3 per cent which had been imposed on a temporary basis in the spring of 1968.
In fact, at that time, the then Minister of Finance, who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), said that this surtax would only be levied in 1968 and 1969.
Ottawa finances are now in a bad way, and what is worse, they are inadequately and inefficiently managed. They are so far from achieving the anticipated results that what is adopted temporarily becomes a sort of habit-unfortunate and unexplainable we must admit- because the government does not plan either on a short term or a long term basis.
We have evidence of it today in this measure designed to extend the social development tax of 3 per cent which had been imposed on a temporary basis. It is a clear indication of the failure of the Liberal administration which is more proficient in the art of provoking and muzzling than in management matters.
Mr. Speaker, a high level of taxation and government revenue per capita is naturally associated with a high level of public expenses per capita, and this would lead us to believe that Canadians should expect more government services.
So today the federal government must justify not only the principle of this 3 per cent increase in taxation but also the use it is being put to.
Having heard the presentations of previous speakers, with the exception of the speech of the hon. member for
Compton (Mr. Latulippe) who showed the other side of the coin, as is seldom done in this House, I say straight out that this government is unable to justify this 3 per cent surcharge.
Mr. Speaker, when this 3 per cent surtax was enacted in the spring of 1968, it was specifically designed to increase governmental revenues so as to enable the government to ensure a marked social development for the community as well as for the individual.
I refer to the speech delivered then by the Minister of Finance who said that without this surtax, the government would not be in a position to ensure social development and that with it, Canadians would be a lot better off.
The result of such a policy is apparent today. Such is truly not the case. This tax, a so-called social development tax, not only has not ensured social development in Canada but, furthermore, it has not provided anything worthwhile to those whose income places them on the threshold of poverty.
The principle of ensuring social development through taxes is, in my humble opinion, basically wrong and, as conclusive evidence, I would say the same thing of any social welfare or guaranteed income legislation which we now hear more and more about and which would only result in increased social welfare expenditures and finally, would not eliminate poverty in Canada, because it gives rise to an unfair increase in taxes based on unfair tax rates. The Finance Minister of King Philip once said: "Give me sound policies and I will give you sound finance."
Not only our financial situation is poor, but our policies are out of focus. It is a basic truth and this is why I feel that a country cannot at the same time indulge in every political trend and fancy, while forgetting the individual needs and its duties, and still believe that the economy will continue to progress.
If the government does not accept its financial and monetary responsibilities, it must not expect that the economy will be prosperous. When we sow poverty we reap poverty. When we pass legislation creating social injustices we create social injustice. When legislation that favors the big man at the expense of the little man is initiated, the result is oppression of the weak by the strong.
Mr. Speaker, naturally I want to oppose strongly the 3 per cent surtax because it advantages the big man, the large companies that crush the small people, regardless of their income.
I will go even further. The philosophy of the central government is unfair, not only to individuals at the benefit of large companies, but also to the provinces whose revenues are limited by the federal government. The policy is also unfair to municipalities that are deprived of that much taxing power.
Today, provincial and municipal governments, instead of trying to meet the needs of the individual by giving him more purchasing power, must fight with the federal government to know who will tax the individual more.

March 3, 1971

Mr. Speaker, the three levels of government all operate on the same fundamentally erroneous policy. Let us take a few minutes to analyze the phenomenon.
Mr. Speaker, when the economy is in full swing, what is the fiscal or monetary policy of governments under the present financial system? The only policy which they advocate is a policy of expansion of investments. As they cannot implement that policy of investments by their sole resources, what do they do? They go to foreign countries to borrow money at high interest rates in order to reinvest in Canada.
But when the economy is recessing, when social progress is not assured, what do those same governments do? Which principles guide them to lead the economy? They do the contrary, by adopting positions of restraint on credit. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was telling to the leaders of the CLC this week: If inflation has caused unemployment, it is because workers have shown unwillingness to tighten their belt. A restraint policy, this is what it means.
When the economy is expanding, instead of financing such development with the tools available to them, government borrow from foreign sources. In so doing, they plunge individuals into debt.
As a matter of fact, if one refers to statistics, he will see that the per capita debt in Canada has been conti-nously on the increase for 25 years, and this because governments never stopped borrowing at exorbitant interest rates.
Such a policy contributes to individuals getting into debt. And while we go through a recession period, governments as I said propose measures of restricted credit, telling everybody: Tighten your belts! Starve to death! We have to prevent galloping inflation! Stop there! Sit quietly, we must avoid galloping inflation! And they adopt measures aimed at restricting credit.
Now, this second item of the government's fiscal policy brings about the same result as the first-indebtedness for individuals. In fact, over a period of economic recession, the individual, while seeing the various governments tighten credit, finds himself obliged to get into debt, for he lacks money. Then the unemployment rate is bound to increase. The individual lacks a stable income. His security is challenged, his freedom of choice lessened. And in such a case, as in the first, again it is the individual who becomes deprived of pm-chasing power, and his indebtedness persists. This explains why the Canadian people have $12 billion worth of debts, entered into with the help of private finance companies which are quite happy when economic crises occur for they can handsomely benefit from them while they provide loans at interest rates ranging from 15 to 25 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, the government therefore has only two means as its disposal to control, administer and guide the economy. Those two means, one of which serves in times of expansion, the other in times of recession, have the same effect, that is to deprive the individual of the purchasing power he needs, fundamentally and vitally, and secondly, to increase his debts.
Income Tax Act
That 3 per cent tax lies at the very heart of the problem. It is the logical result of an administration basically distorted that fits, it must be said, into the context of a poor administration.
Mr. Speaker, as recorded on page 7394 of Hansard of March 7, 1968 the then Minister of Finance said, at the time the 3 per cent surtax was implemented, that this tax would only apply to 1968-69 to solve an immediate problem.
The mere fact that the government is extending this tax proves that its policy is no good.
The Minister of Finance of the central government made a mistake and this is why today the government must impose again this tax with a new "song".
In 1968, the 3 per cent surtax for individuals was expected to yield $105 million during fiscal year 1968-69, but it was not necessarily applied to corporations since this was to produce only $45 million.
These figures are supplied by the ministers of Finance themselves and they prove that this 3 per cent surtax did not apply to those able to pay it but rather to those who had no choice and whose income was inadequate.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the premises I have just stated, the government's policies during expansion or slowdown periods inevitably contribute to increase the debts of the individual. In fact, this tax applies to the individual and not to the big companies. With this tax, the government is once again adding to the burden of the individual, the family man, the worker and the farmer.
Mr. Speaker, the 3 per cent surtax is not quite fair in our present system. Let us suppose-what I will never admit-that the present tax table is fair, this tax is still more unjust than the present tax table. At least the latter takes into account a certain income scale, while the 3 per cent tax equally applies to all individuals, regardless of their income, the number of their children or their responsibilities and needs.
Mr. Speaker, this tax is disgusting. Moreover, the surtax levied in 1968 was levied in an allegedly inflationary period, but according to the Prime Minister, we are not going through such a period at the present time. The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister boast of having checked inflation and when this 3 per cent tax was established, they both said that surtax was to be levied at all costs, since it would help to check inflation.
Mr. Speaker, if we are to believe the Prime Minister's words, inflation today has been checked. Therefore, why a 3 per cent tax? Either the Minister of Finance lied in the spring of 1968 or today's minister is also a liar. But a decision has to be taken. If inflation was really checked, has he any reason today for keeping that 3 per cent tax? If it has not been checked, it means a 3 per cent tax was levied upon us in 1968 under false representations and the government should therefore give back to every taxpayer the money thus wrongly collected.
Those are but idle dreams really, for the government is using that to beguile people, so as to make them forget the real problem.

Mr. Speaker, whenever there is an economic recession, this government like its predecessors adopts measures to restrict credit. We say that it is precisely at such a time that the government should do something, through the use of two monetary and fiscal instruments, easily controllable, respecting individual freedom and security, namely the compensated discount on prices.
When the economy is expanding, the government should resort to what we call the national dividend.
The national dividend and compensated discount are the only two tools which, while respecting the liberty and security of individuals and adapting to their needs, allow them to really take part in the economy, to get their share of production, while avoiding economic recessions or the notorious economic cycle we know constantly, namely inflation or recession.
For these reasons, I am totally opposed to this so-called 3 per cent social development tax which has not really produced social progress but rather the recession of our economy, especially of individuals.
Mr. Speaker, in a twelve month period of application, according to the present Minister of Finance, it is expected that this tax will bring in $245 million. Experience has shown repeatedly that the present legislation is not strict enough with respect to companies and firms and to capital costs.
The present legislation on capital costs favours industry too much rather than the individual, and the bill before us today will result in a direct improvement of a situation which is already too beneficial to the big ones, that is, to those who already have a strong position in the economy, against those who are destitute. The bill introduced today by the Minister of Finance is aimed at encouraging new investments, and the tax paid by companies concerned will be reduced for a certain number of years by something like $250 million. Next year for instance, the reduction will amount to $25 million.
This bill has been introduced for the benefit of major companies and at the expense of individual citizens, householders and all those who now need government help to live.
In 1968, some 36 per cent of all individual citizens who had paid income tax were not concerned with the 3 per cent surtax. In 1971, because of these new principles of the Minister of Finance, only 25 per cent of Canadian taxpayers will be exempt.
Therefore, the 3 per cent surtax imposed by the government today is not exactly the same it has levied in the spring of 1968. Thus it modifies the aims set up in 1968; this is another indirect way, not to levy 3 per cent, but in fact 6 per cent on income because, owing to the renewal of the former 3 per cent tax, more individuals will be touched and fewer companies will be affected.
The government's need for money has obviously increased today. Before this bill is passed, we might wonder, whether the result of government policy, financed with millions of dollars, is really what was expected.
Mr. Speaker, when we look at the social, economic and fiscal situation of Canadians we soon realize that the results in the field of the socail policy of the liberal government have fallen short of the results which had been anticipated, and that poverty and misery have worsened in a country glutted with riches.
The wealth of a country, or its sound economic productivity should not be assessed according to its resources, since a country may have great resources and great poverty.
The value of the economy should be assessed according to the brains used to administer it. If there is still some gray matter left on the other side of the House, let them use it to make the economy serve Canadians and stop levying taxes and surtaxes. Heavens knows what kind of tax they can dream up to increase revenues. Let them stop crushing the small Canadian taxpayers and at last give them the opportunity to participate in the economy.
We are making today another attempt to protest against the levying of the so-called social development tax of 3 per cent because it was levied on false pretenses, and did not produce the results anticipated. Since this tax is not warranted, the government should save us from it.
Mr. Speaker, we are taking this opportunity to show our colleagues we are floundering in this financial system, that all these measures mean nothing and only aggravate the economic situation of the country.
Mr. Speaker, we urge our colleagues seriously to consider the Social Credit theory and the solutions it proposes, namely, use the Bank of Canada to advance the necessary credit to all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal, in order to really finance social progress at the public sector level without putting the Canadian taxpayers into debt.
Today, to finance their investments, the governments have to get the Canadians into debt, depriving them of the minimum purchasing power. We suggest that they use the Bank of Canada to finance social development, to support the policy of the federal, provincial and municipal governments, in order to pay for only one school, only one bridge. We must no longer have to pay for three schools: two for finance, and one for us.
That is what makes the taxes go up. Interest mars the loans of the government, and by borrowing it does not use the tools at its disposal. All it has to do is to decide, but it continues to get the Canadians deeper into debt. We urge the government to use the Bank of Canada to finance the public sector on the basis of the true value of the goods produced, the real credit, so that our country might achieve a decent, progressive growth, without getting the Canadians into debt.
